feed.title: Mount Fuji

image.credit: Romain Guy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Mount Fuji is an active stratovolcano on the island of Honshu, about 100 kilometres southwest of Tokyo, with a summit at 3,776 metres. It last erupted in 1707–1708. The present cone sits on older volcanoes, including Ko-Fuji, which formed between 100,000 and 17,000 years ago and is now almost completely buried. Its symmetrical cone is covered in snow for about five months of the year, and it joined the World Heritage List as a cultural site in 2013. This photograph was taken at 17:49 on 19 March 2025 from Lake Kawaguchi, the lowest of the Fuji Five Lakes, whose shore is popular with photographers for its panoramic views of the mountain.
feed.lookAt: The lake is smoothed to glass and the clouds are dragged into soft streaks: this is a long exposure, seconds rather than fractions. That stillness leaves the snowy cone as the only crisp form. The shoreline sits on the lower third, handing most of the frame to the sky's gradient from blue to sunset gold.

feed.title: Elgin Bridge

image.credit: Frank Schulenburg, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Elgin Bridge carries traffic across the Singapore River between the Downtown Core and the Singapore River Planning Area. It stands on the site of the river's first crossing, a wooden footbridge of 1822 built after Stamford Raffles asked for a bridge linking the communities on either bank. An iron bridge named after the 8th Earl of Elgin replaced it in 1862, and the present concrete bridge was opened by Governor Sir Hugh Clifford on 30 May 1929. The Italian sculptor Rudolfo Nolli designed its cast-iron lamps. In 2019 it was gazetted a National Monument with the Anderson and Cavenagh bridges. Frank Schulenburg made this long exposure during blue hour on 18 August 2023 as a boat passed underneath.
feed.lookAt: The boat is gone, but its path stays: a long exposure turned it into red and green streaks sweeping out of the left edge. Everything static stays sharp, from the lit arch to the railing. That railing on the right is a leading line, pulling your eye from the foreground into the frame.

feed.title: The Tetons and the Snake River

image.credit: Ansel Adams, U.S. National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams made The Tetons and the Snake River in 1942 in Grand Teton National Park, Wyoming. It belongs to the Mural Project: in 1941 the National Park Service contracted him for 180 days to photograph parks, Indian reservations and other places the Interior Department managed, for mural-sized prints to decorate the department's new building. The project ended on June 30, 1942, and because of the war the murals were never made. Adams sent 225 small prints and held on to the 229 negatives. He had helped found Group f/64, which favoured sharp focus and the full tonal range, and with Fred Archer had recently worked out the Zone System for controlling exposure and development. The picture was later encoded on the Voyager Golden Record.
feed.lookAt: The river enters at the bottom and swings out to the middle left, an S that walks your eye from near to far; Adams stood high on a bluff so the bend reads as a shape. Black pines and white snow both keep detail. Expose for both ends, then wait for broken cloud to light the water.

caption.title: The Tetons and the Snake River

feed.title: Mount Lu

image.credit: pfctdayelise, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Mount Lu, or Lushan, rises in Jiujiang, Jiangxi province, with the Yangtze River to the north and Poyang Lake to the east. The oval massif is about 25 kilometres long, and its highest point, Dahanyang Peak, reaches 1,474 metres. Its steep peaks stand above a sea of clouds that can surround the mountain for almost 200 days each year. Buddhist and Daoist temples and Confucian landmarks made it one of China's spiritual centres, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996. The Song dynasty poet Su Shi wrote that he could not tell Lushan's true shape because he was inside the mountain. This photograph was taken in winter 2005; the pines are Huangshan pine.
feed.lookAt: Fog does the layering. The ridge on the right is near-black and full of texture; the cliff on the left is paler and softer; the gap between dissolves to white. Each step back loses contrast, and that loss reads as depth. The pines silhouetted along the right edge give scale, and the vertical frame stacks cliff over void.

feed.title: Monster Building

image.credit: Benh LIEU SONG, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The so-called Monster Building is a group of five connected residential blocks on King's Road in Quarry Bay, Hong Kong. Built in the 1960s as Parker Estate, named after nearby Mount Parker, it was split in 1972 into the Fook Cheong, Montane, Oceanic, Yick Cheong and Yick Fat buildings. Its 2,243 flats house about 10,000 people. The estate became a magnet for photographers after a picture of it by Romain Jacquet-Lagrèze spread widely in 2013, and residents now post signs asking visitors to be respectful. It has appeared in films such as Ghost in the Shell. Benh Lieu Song looked straight up at the Yick Cheong Building at night on 13 June 2019.
feed.lookAt: Pointing the camera straight up turns walls into a frame. The building faces close in from both sides, leaving a column of violet sky as the only empty space, and a tower rises into it from the bottom. Thousands of windows and air conditioners become texture; the calm gap is what gives them shape.

feed.title: White House Ruin — view of cliff dwelling from river valley, in "Canyon de Chelly" National Monument, Arizona

image.credit: Ansel Adams, U.S. National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams made this vertical view of the White House Ruin for the Mural Project, his 1941–42 contract with the National Park Service to photograph places the Interior Department managed for mural-sized prints. The murals were never made because of the war; the National Archives holds the series as Ansel Adams Photographs of National Parks and Monuments. Canyon de Chelly, in northeastern Arizona, became a National Park Service unit in 1931. It lies inside the Navajo Nation, is owned by the Navajo Tribal Trust, and preserves ruins of peoples from the Ancestral Puebloans to the Navajo. About forty Navajo families live in the park, and visitors may enter the canyons only with a ranger or Navajo guide, except on the White House Ruin Trail.
feed.lookAt: The ruin takes only a strip in the lower third; the cliff fills everything above it, its dark streaks pouring down toward the rooms. That is how the vertical frame gives scale. Light skims the wall so every crack carries texture, while the alcove goes nearly black. Let the setting dwarf your subject.

feed.title: Chola Lake

image.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Chola Lake is a glacial lake at about 4,600 metres in the Chola Valley of Nepal's Khumbu region, south of the Great Himalayan Range. It lies beneath the north wall of the Cholatse–Taboche massif. The Chola glacier descends from Cholatse's east face, and the name is literal: in Tibetan 'cho' is lake, 'la' is pass and 'tse' is peak. Cholatse's north and east faces can be seen from Dughla, on the trail to Everest base camp; the mountain was first climbed on 22 April 1982. Vyacheslav Argenberg took this photograph on 18 October 2009, with alluvial fans and glacial moraines running down to the water under a blanket of cloud.
feed.lookAt: The lichen-covered boulder at bottom centre is the anchor. It gives the eye something near, tells you that you are standing high above the water, and closes the lower edge. From it the turquoise shoreline curves right into the grey fans, while the cloud lid hides the summits and keeps attention on texture.

feed.title: Angkor Wat

image.credit: Satdeep Gill, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Angkor Wat, in Siem Reap, Cambodia, is the largest religious complex in the world, on a site of 162.6 hectares. The Khmer king Suryavarman II built it in the first half of the 12th century as a Hindu temple to Vishnu, probably intended as his mausoleum. From the late 13th century it gradually became a Buddhist temple, and it has remained in use ever since. Its plan represents Mount Meru: galleries rise towards a central quincunx of towers, the highest reaching 65 metres. Unusually, it faces west. Angkor was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992, and the temple appears on Cambodia's flag. Satdeep Gill photographed it with its reflection on 9 September 2022.
feed.lookAt: The horizon sits almost exactly in the middle, which usually feels static, but here it is the point: the pool repeats the towers upside down, so the frame becomes a mirror. Notice the reflection is darker and softer than the temple. Calm water and a low position make the double image possible.

feed.title: Earthrise

image.credit: William Anders, NASA, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: William Anders took Earthrise on December 24, 1968, from lunar orbit during Apollo 8, the first crewed voyage to orbit the Moon. He was using a heavily modified Hasselblad 500 EL with an electric drive, a simple sighting ring instead of a reflex viewfinder, and a 250 mm lens he had been using to photograph the lunar surface. When Earth appeared over the horizon he called for a roll of colour film, quickly; Jim Lovell noted the setting, 1/250 second at f/11. The custom Ektachrome was processed after the crew returned. The published version is rotated 95 degrees clockwise from the original so that Earth appears to rise. Nature photographer Galen Rowell called it the most influential environmental photograph ever taken.
feed.lookAt: Earth is small, just right of centre, and almost the whole square is black. The lunar horizon runs as a tilted grey band across the bottom fifth. The emptiness is what makes the planet matter. When your subject is distant, resist zooming tight: give it space and one edge to rise from.

feed.title: Moraine Lake

image.credit: Gorgo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Moraine Lake is a snow- and glacier-fed alpine lake in Banff National Park, Alberta, 14 kilometres from the village of Lake Louise. It sits in the Valley of the Ten Peaks at about 1,884 metres and covers 50 hectares. Because it fills almost entirely from melt, it does not reach its crest until middle to late June; when full, rock sediment washed in by the surrounding glaciers gives it its azure colour. The lake has never been dammed or drained. Since 2023 the road has been closed to private cars. This photograph was taken on 17 September 2005; the peaks include Mount Allen, Mount Tuzo, Deltaform Mountain and Neptuak Mountain.
feed.lookAt: The shoreline sits just below the middle, so the reflection carries almost as much weight as the peaks themselves. Dead-still water and a low vantage at the lake's edge make the mirror. Sunlight rakes across the cliff faces and picks out every horizontal ledge, while the scree slope at left falls into cool shadow.

feed.title: Mosque of Ibn Tulun

image.credit: Berthold Werner, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Mosque of Ibn Tulun in Islamic Cairo is the oldest well-preserved mosque in Egypt. Ahmad ibn Tulun, the Abbasid governor who made himself Egypt's de facto ruler, built it between 876 and 879 as the congregational mosque of his new capital, al-Qata'i. Its design follows the mosques of Samarra in Iraq, and its minaret has an unusual external spiral staircase. When al-Qata'i was razed in 905, the mosque was spared, and it is the city's only surviving monument. The domed fountain kiosk at the centre of the courtyard dates from a restoration by the Mamluk sultan Lajin in 1296. Berthold Werner photographed the courtyard on 4 November 2010.
feed.lookAt: Two buildings, two distances. The domed kiosk fills the centre and the spiral minaret stands back on the left, so you read depth without any lines leading in. Low arcades run across the whole width like a baseline, their dark arches repeating a rhythm. The empty plain sky lets both silhouettes read cleanly.

feed.title: Farmer and sons walking in the face of a dust storm. Cimarron County, Oklahoma

image.credit: Arthur Rothstein, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arthur Rothstein was 21 when he made this photograph in April 1936 on a farm near Felt, in Cimarron County, Oklahoma. Roy Stryker, his former teacher at Columbia, had hired him to set up the darkroom of the Resettlement Administration's photo unit and then sent him out as its first photographer, to document rural poverty for a New Deal agency. The farmer was Arthur Coble, walking with his young sons Milton and Darrel past fence posts almost buried in dust. Some have claimed the scene was staged; the Cobles said it was not. The agency became the Farm Security Administration in 1937, and the picture became one of the defining images of the Dust Bowl.
feed.lookAt: There is no horizon: dust has turned sky and ground into one grey, so the dark shed and three figures float in a field of tone. Fence posts sunk to stubs in the foreground measure how deep the dust is. In bad weather, look for one dark shape against the flat light.

caption.title: Farmer and Sons in a Dust Storm

feed.title: Cuernos del Paine

image.credit: Pedro Szekely from Los Angeles, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Cuernos del Paine, the 'Horns of Paine', belong to the Cordillera Paine in Torres del Paine National Park, Chilean Patagonia, about 280 kilometres north of Punta Arenas. The range formed about 12.5 million years ago, when magma intruded Cretaceous sedimentary rock and cooled as a laccolith that glaciers later carved. On the Cuernos, pale bands of exposed granite contrast with dark tops, the remnants of an eroded sedimentary layer. Paine means 'blue' in the Tehuelche language. The park was established in 1959 and became a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 1978. Pedro Szekely took this photograph in March 2023, looking at the Cuernos from Lake Pehoé.
feed.lookAt: Low sun from the left strikes only the pale granite faces and the underside of the cloud, so the horns glow while their dark caps stay dark: the two-tone geology made visible by light. Below sit calm bands of shrub and water, with a row of birds on the lake as a small foreground event.

feed.title: Machu Picchu

image.credit: Martin St-Amant, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel on a mountain ridge 2,430 metres up in southern Peru, about 80 kilometres northwest of Cusco, above the Urubamba River. It is thought to have been built around 1450 as an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti, and it was abandoned about a century later, probably during the Spanish conquest. Its finely fitted dry-stone walls are in the classical Inca style. The site sits on a saddle between two peaks, Machu Picchu and Huayna Picchu, the steep mountain behind the ruins. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983. Martin St-Amant took this photograph on 27 June 2009; the file page describes it as Machu Picchu at twilight.
feed.lookAt: Light is selective here. Low sun picks out the terraces and the green plaza while the mountains behind stay in shadow, and the heavy cloud above presses everything down. That contrast is why the ruins jump forward. Stand high, keep the peak behind your subject, and wait for light that singles it out.

feed.title: Grain elevators along the route of the Atchison, Topeka, and Santa Fe Railroad, Amarillo, Texas

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano made this colour transparency in March 1943 in Amarillo, Texas; the agency caption calls it part of a Santa Fe trip along the railroad's route. Born Yakov Ovcharov in 1914 in what is now Ukraine, he emigrated to the United States in 1923 and studied art in Philadelphia. Roy Stryker hired him in 1940 for the Farm Security Administration's photography program, at $2,300 a year, on condition that he own a car and a driver's licence. Delano tended to photograph the cultural and social patterns of regions rather than people or landscape alone, and by the time the country entered the war he had made photo essays on American industry. The slide came to the Library of Congress from the Office of War Information in 1944.
feed.lookAt: Delano stood far back and square-on, so the silos read as one flat wall of repeated cylinders with the painted names across them. The horizon sits below centre, giving the streaked sky more than half the frame, and a lone pole breaks the rhythm. When a building's power is repetition, face it straight.

feed.title: Deadvlei

image.credit: Giles Laurent, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Deadvlei is a white clay pan near Sossusvlei, in Namibia's Namib-Naukluft Park. Its name means 'dead marsh', from English and the Afrikaans vlei. The pan formed when the Tsauchab River flooded after rain, leaving shallow pools where camel thorn trees could grow. When drought came and sand dunes encroached, the river was cut off and the trees died, believed to be 600 to 700 years ago. The wood is not petrified, but it has not decomposed because the area is so dry. The surrounding dunes reach 300 to 400 metres. Giles Laurent photographed this dead camel thorn tree, Vachellia erioloba, on the morning of 24 July 2025.
feed.lookAt: Three flat bands, white pan, orange dune and blue sky, and one dark shape cutting through all of them. The tree is centred, which usually feels static, but the symmetry suits this stillness. Morning sun from the left throws its shadow right across the pan, and the dune's lit and shaded slopes give the backdrop depth.

feed.title: Charles Bridge

image.credit: DXR, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Charles Bridge is a medieval stone arch bridge across the Vltava in Prague. Construction began in 1357 under King Charles IV to replace the Judith Bridge, badly damaged by a flood in 1342. Legend says the first stone was laid at 5:31 on 9 July 1357, a palindromic moment chosen by the numerology-minded emperor. Until 1841 it was the only way across the river, linking Prague Castle with the Old Town on the coronation route of Bohemian kings. It is 516 metres long, rests on 16 arches and is lined with 30 statues, now all replicas. DXR photographed it from the neighbouring Mánes Bridge at about six in the evening on 8 August 2016.
feed.lookAt: The famous bridge is small here, a dark line of arches on the right. Shooting from the neighbouring bridge gives it context: river, boats, the dark tower at its end and the city's domes. The sky takes half the frame because the clouds earn it. Sometimes the best view of a landmark is from beside it.

feed.title: Filling station and garage at Pie Town, New Mexico

image.credit: Russell Lee, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Russell Lee made this colour slide in October 1940 in Pie Town, a homesteading community on U.S. Highway 60 in Catron County, New Mexico; the record notes that the town's original owner sold pies, hence the name. Lee had trained as a chemical engineer, turned to painting, and took up photography first as a reference tool. Roy Stryker hired him for the Farm Security Administration's documentary project in the fall of 1936. His Pie Town series, which used Kodachrome colour film, became one of his best-known bodies of work, and in black and white he was known for using direct flash in interiors other photographers avoided. The slide was transferred to the Library of Congress from the Office of War Information in 1944.
feed.lookAt: The rounded edge of the slide mount is still in the frame. Two red pumps stand just right of centre, echoing the red band of siding above, while men and a truck balance the left. In colour, let one strong hue repeat across the frame against neutral white, brown and sky.

feed.title: Skaftafellsjökull

image.credit: Martin Falbisoner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Skaftafellsjökull is a glacier spur of the Vatnajökull ice cap at Skaftafell, southeast Iceland. Skaftafell became a national park on 15 September 1967 and joined the larger Vatnajökull National Park on 7 June 2008. Its landscape has been shaped by eruptions of Öræfajökull and by glaciers and rivers; eruptions under the ice can trigger glacial floods, jökulhlaups, which spread sand across the Skeiðarársandur outwash plain. An eruption of Öræfajökull in 1362 wiped out the local community, and the district has been called Öræfi, 'the wasteland', ever since. Martin Falbisoner took this photograph on 21 July 2014 from the Skaftafellsheiði plateau, above the glacier's terminus, its lake and the river Skeiðará.
feed.lookAt: The hikers on the rocky outcrop make the picture: without them the ice, lake and plain have no scale. Placed low and central, they also stand in for you, looking in. Flat overcast light keeps the dark ice ridges and grey water evenly exposed, and the lake's curving edge leads toward the braided rivers at right.

feed.title: Brooklyn Bridge

image.credit: Carlos Delgado, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Brooklyn Bridge spans the East River between Manhattan and Brooklyn. Designed by John A. Roebling, with his son Washington Roebling as chief engineer, assisted by Emily Warren Roebling, it took thirteen years to build and opened on 24 May 1883. It was the first fixed crossing of the East River and, with a main span of 486.3 metres, the longest suspension bridge in the world at the time. Its hybrid design uses both vertical and diagonal cables, hung from neo-Gothic stone towers with pointed arches. Carlos Delgado took this night photograph in July 2012 for Wiki Loves Monuments, with the Freedom Tower, then under construction, and 8 Spruce Street behind.
feed.lookAt: A slow shutter erased the cars and kept their lights: white and amber streaks run along the roadway toward the stone tower. Above them, the cables and steel crossbeams make a net of lines that all converge on that pointed arch. Fixed geometry plus moving light is the classic night-bridge recipe.

feed.title: Chrysler Building detail, New York, New York

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith photographed the crown of the Chrysler Building on September 16, 2007. Since 1992 she has given her pictures of American places to the Library of Congress, nearly 100,000 images placed in the public domain, following the example of Frances Benjamin Johnston, who also donated her life's work there. This frame is born digital, part of Carol M. Highsmith's America, which the Library acquired in 2009. The building, designed by William Van Alen and finished in 1930, has a terraced crown of seven radiating arches clad in Nirosta stainless steel with triangular windows. Its 125-foot spire was built secretly inside the frame and raised on October 23, 1929; the building was the world's tallest for 11 months.
feed.lookAt: The verticals stay parallel; seen from the street below, the tower would lean backward. Sun catches the steel arches on one side, the other falls to grey, so the crown reads in relief against a deep blue sky. Get distance and height, not a wide lens, to keep architecture upright.

caption.title: Chrysler Building Crown
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Lake Hāwea

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Lake Hāwea lies in the Otago Region of New Zealand's South Island, at 348 metres above sea level. It stretches 35 kilometres from north to south, covers about 151 square kilometres and is 392 metres deep. It fills a glacial valley formed during the last ice age and is dammed at its southern end by a terminal moraine about 10,000 years old. In 1958 the lake was raised 20 metres to store water for hydroelectric power at the Roxburgh Dam. Lake Wānaka lies in a parallel glacial valley 8 kilometres to the west. The lake is named after a Māori tribe who preceded the Waitaha people. Michal Klajban took this photograph at 08:42 on 4 April 2019.
feed.lookAt: This is about timing. Shafts of sun break through the cloud and fall as pale columns between the ridges, lighting the mist over the water; minutes later they would be gone. Exposing for the bright cloud lets the mountains sink toward silhouette, and the thin strip of lake keeps the horizon low, leaving the drama overhead.

feed.title: Sydney Opera House

image.credit: Diliff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Sydney Opera House occupies the whole of Bennelong Point on Sydney Harbour. The Danish architect Jørn Utzon won an international design competition in 1957, and the New South Wales government authorised work to begin the following year. Cost and schedule overruns followed, Utzon resigned, and an Australian team led by Peter Hall completed the building. Queen Elizabeth II opened it on 20 October 1973. Its roof is a series of precast concrete shells, each made from sections of a sphere 75.2 metres in radius. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007. Diliff took this exposure-blended photograph from the Sydney Harbour Bridge on 2 December 2008, using a Canon 5D and a 100mm lens.
feed.lookAt: A 100mm lens from the Harbour Bridge compresses the scene: the shells, the waterfront and the city lights behind seem stacked close together. Seen from above and to the side, the shells overlap like fanned sails. Blending exposures kept detail in the bright white roofs and in the dark harbour at once.

feed.title: Pike and Henry Streets, Manhattan

image.credit: Berenice Abbott, New York Public Library, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Berenice Abbott made this view down Pike Street toward the Manhattan Bridge on March 6, 1936, for Changing New York. She had returned to New York in 1929 after years in Paris, where she had bought the remainder of Eugène Atget's archive, and set out to record the city as it turned into a modern metropolis, working with an 8 × 10-inch Century Universal view camera. In 1935 the Federal Art Project hired her as supervisor of the project, which let her hire assistants and concentrate on photographing and printing. By her resignation in 1939 she had produced 305 photographs, and a book of the series appeared that year with captions by Elizabeth McCausland. She favoured natural light, careful composition and sharp focus.
feed.lookAt: Tenement walls and their fire escapes funnel to the bridge tower, framed in the gap at the end of the street. Haze pales the tower, so the distance reads as layers. Shadow fills the left foreground while sun lands on the right pavement. Look for streets that frame a landmark, and shoot when air adds depth.

feed.title: Serengeti at Sunrise

image.credit: Giles Laurent, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Serengeti is a geographical region in Africa, spanning the Mara and Arusha Regions of Tanzania and extending to southwestern Kenya. The protected area within it covers about 30,000 square kilometres, including Serengeti National Park and several game reserves. It hosts one of the world's largest land animal migrations by total body weight, and is counted among the Seven Natural Wonders of Africa. Its habitats include riverine forests, swamps, kopjes, grasslands and woodlands, and about 70 large mammal and 500 bird species live there. The name is often said to come from the Maa word "seringit", meaning "endless plains", though that etymology does not appear in Maa dictionaries. This panorama was taken at 05:02 on 9 July 2020, in the golden hour of sunrise.
feed.lookAt: A 140 mm lens with a teleconverter squeezes the low hill and the distant horizon into a thin band, leaving the grass to fill most of the frame. Early sunlight rakes across the seed heads and turns each tuft gold while the sky stays a cool violet. Look for that warm-against-cool contrast in the first minutes after sunrise.

feed.title: Dune 45

image.credit: Giles Laurent, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Dune 45 stands in the southern part of the Namib Desert, in the Namib-Naukluft National Park of Namibia. It is so called because it lies 45 kilometres past Sesriem on the road to Sossusvlei. The dune is 80 metres high and is composed of 5-million-year-old sands. The photographer's file description says it is made of iron-rich quartz sand, whose deepening red tones come from gradual oxidation. That sand began as sediment carried by the Orange River to the Atlantic, was moved north by coastal currents, and was blown inland by south-westerly winds. This frame was taken at 08:39 on 24 July 2025 with a 70–200 mm lens set to 113 mm.
feed.lookAt: The sun rakes in from the left, so the ridge becomes one hard, curving line that splits the dune into red light and blue-black shadow. That edge is the whole composition. A 113 mm focal length flattens the slope into a clean shape, and tiny acacias at its base give the scale.

feed.title: Looking East Down Clay Street

image.credit: Arnold Genthe, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arnold Genthe made this photograph on 18 April 1906, looking east down Clay Street at the Great Fire in San Francisco. Genthe was born in Berlin and arrived in San Francisco in 1895 to work as a tutor, teaching himself photography afterwards. He was intrigued by the Chinese section of the city and photographed its inhabitants; about 200 of his Chinatown pictures survive. The earthquake and fire destroyed his studio, but he rebuilt. The Library of Congress holds this 4 × 5 inch lantern slide under digital ID cph.3c36175, and Genthe published the picture in his 1936 book As I Remember.
feed.lookAt: Two figures stand in the foreground with their backs to you, so you look over their shoulders at the fire. The steep street leads up to a bright smoke cloud, and the dark foreground against the light centre guides the eye. When something big happens, put people in front of it, so the viewer stands where they stand.

feed.title: Matterhorn and the Milky Way

image.credit: Giles Laurent, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Matterhorn is a mountain of the Alps on the border between Switzerland and Italy, a near-symmetric pyramidal peak in the Pennine Alps whose summit is 4,478 metres above sea level. It has four faces, separated by the Hörnli, Furggen, Zmutt and Leone ridges, and overlooks the Swiss town of Zermatt. Edward Whymper's party made the first ascent on 14 July 1865, and four climbers fell to their deaths on the descent. The peak is mainly gneiss that began as fragments of the African plate. The photographer says this picture needed months of waiting for clear skies, a new moon and the Milky Way passing behind the summit. Those conditions met on 20 August 2023, and he waited until about 3 a.m.
feed.lookAt: Plan first, then wait. Phone apps predicted the night the Milky Way would stand behind the summit, and the shutter then stayed open for 8 seconds at f/1.4 on a 24 mm lens. The still lake doubles both peak and stars, and the vertical format gives the sky most of the frame. Plan the shot around the sky.

feed.title: Tianzi Mountain, Wulingyuan

image.credit: chensiyuan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Wulingyuan is a scenic and historical site in Hunan Province in South Central China, noted for more than 3,000 quartzite sandstone pillars and peaks, many over 200 metres high, along with ravines, gorges, streams and waterfalls. It lies in Zhangjiajie City, about 270 kilometres northwest of Changsha, and covers 690 square kilometres. It is made up of four parks, including the Tianzi Mountain Nature Reserve. The pillars formed during the Devonian period, 400 to 350 million years ago, through a combination of tectonic uplift and water erosion. UNESCO inscribed the site in 1992. This panorama was taken from Mount Tianzi Shan; it is a featured picture on Commons, and its metadata dates it to 9 October 2012.
feed.lookAt: Haze does the compositional work here. Each ridge of pillars is paler and bluer than the one in front, so depth reads as stacked layers. A 17 mm lens keeps the foreground trees large and the distant ridges small. Find a viewpoint above the valley and let atmospheric haze separate the planes.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wulingyuan Scenic and Historic Interest Area

feed.title: Half Dome, Yosemite Valley

image.credit: Carleton Watkins, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carleton Watkins made this albumen print of Half Dome around 1865. He was born in 1829, and in July 1861 he travelled to Yosemite with his mammoth-plate camera, which used 18 × 22 inch glass plates, and his stereoscopic camera. He returned with thirty mammoth plates and one hundred stereoview negatives. It is said that Senator John Conness passed Watkins' photographs around Congress, one of the major factors in Lincoln signing the Yosemite Grant in 1864. Wikipedia says his photographs brought Half Dome to people. His studio was destroyed in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire. The Library of Congress holds this print under digital ID ppmsca.09985.
feed.lookAt: The camera stands on a ledge, and the rock edge at lower right gives a foreground that makes the drop feel real. The dark valley floor and pale far ridges separate by tone alone, and the dome catches the light at top right. Get on a ledge, include the near rock, and let tone create the distance.

feed.title: Sildpollnes Church, Lofoten

image.credit: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: 169 km north of the Arctic Circle

feed.story: Lofoten is an archipelago and traditional district in Nordland county, Norway, with dramatic mountains and peaks, open sea and sheltered bays, beaches and untouched lands. It has two towns, Svolvær and Leknes, and Leknes lies about 169 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle. Winter temperatures are extremely mild for the latitude, possibly the largest positive temperature anomaly in the world relative to latitude. This view looks across Austnesfjorden to Sildpollnes Church, on the Sildpollnes peninsula of the island of Austvågøya. It was taken at 22:11 on 26 April 2015 and is a panorama of several frames merged in software using a cylindrical projection.
feed.lookAt: A small white church with a red roof sits at the left edge, and its size tells you how tall the snowy peaks really are. Dry grass in the foreground leads the eye to the water. Late-evening cloud keeps the light soft and blue, so the church's warm colours are the only bright note.

feed.title: Kolmanskop Doorway

image.credit: James Kerwin Photographic, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kolmanskop, Afrikaans for "Coleman's peak", is a ghost town in the Namib in southern Namibia, 10 kilometres inland from the port of Lüderitz. In 1908, in what was then German South-West Africa, railway worker Zacharias Lewala found a diamond and showed it to his supervisor, the German railway inspector August Stauch. German miners settled, and residents built the village in the style of a German town, with a hospital, ballroom, power station, casino and ice factory, the first x-ray station in the southern hemisphere and the first tram in Africa. The diamond field began to deplete during World War I, and the town was abandoned in 1956. Tourists now walk through houses knee-deep in sand, and need a permit to enter.
feed.lookAt: Doorways inside doorways make a tunnel of frames, each smaller and lit differently, so the eye travels to the leaning door at the centre. The sand rising through the rooms is a diagonal that breaks the symmetry. Stand square to the wall, keep the camera level, and let soft window light fall evenly on the peeling paint.

feed.title: Old Faithful Geyser

image.credit: Ansel Adams, U.S. National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: This photograph of Old Faithful erupting against a dark sky is by Ansel Adams (1902–1984). It belongs to the series Ansel Adams Photographs of National Parks and Monuments, compiled 1941–1942 and documenting the period around 1933 to 1942; the file page gives no exact date. The National Archives holds it in Record Group 79, records of the National Park Service, as 79-AA-T04 (NAID 519994). Old Faithful is a cone geyser in Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming, named in 1870 during the Washburn–Langford–Doane Expedition. It erupts on average every 92 minutes, for 1½ to 5 minutes, to a height of 106 to 185 feet.
feed.lookAt: The sky is almost black while the steam is bright white, so the plume stands out like a solid shape. Adams lets the cloud take most of the frame and leaves only a thin strip of textured ground for scale. Wait for the eruption, expose for the steam highlights, and let the sky fall dark.

feed.title: Ama Dablam

image.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ama Dablam is a mountain in the Eastern Himalayas in Koshi Province, Nepal, in the Khumbu. Its main peak is 6,812 metres high and the lower western peak is 6,170 metres. The name literally means "mother's charm box" in the Sherpa language. Because of its soaring ridges and steep faces, it is sometimes called the "Matterhorn of the Himalayas". The first successful ascent was made on 13 March 1961, when Mike Gill and Barry Bishop were joined by Mike Ward and Wally Romanes, who climbed the Southwest Ridge. This photograph, a northwest view from Pheriche, Nepal, was taken on 20 October 2009.
feed.lookAt: Midday sun lights the snow faces almost flat, so the shape comes from the ridgelines and the shadowed rock beside them. The dark, empty foreground and the low stone wall give the peak a size reference. A deep blue sky is the only backdrop needed to frame so much white.

feed.title: Aoraki / Mount Cook

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Aoraki / Mount Cook is the highest mountain in New Zealand, listed in 2014 at 3,724 metres, in the Southern Alps of the South Island. It has three summits, the Low Peak, Middle Peak and High Peak, with the Tasman Glacier to the east and the Hooker Glacier to the southwest. The English name was given in 1851 by Captain John Lort Stokes to honour Captain James Cook. The first known ascent was on 25 December 1894, by Tom Fyfe, Jack Clarke and George Graham. On 14 December 1991, roughly 12 to 14 million cubic metres of rock and ice fell off the northern peak. This photograph was taken from the upper parts of the track to Mueller Hut on 16 January 2020.
feed.lookAt: From above the valley, layers appear: sunlit snow on the summit, blue mid-ridges, then dark slopes in shade. Haze softens the distance so the eye can separate each ridge. The pale lake and thin river below show where the valley floor falls away. A high viewpoint turns mountains into stacked planes of tone.

feed.title: Manhattan Skyline, South Street and Jones Lane

image.credit: Berenice Abbott, New York Public Library, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Berenice Abbott made this photograph on 26 March 1936 from East River Pier 11, looking toward South Street and Jones Lane in Manhattan. It shows 120 Wall Street at far right and 40 Wall Street, with its pointed top, in the centre, plus signs for Wallrope, McMillan Shackle Blocks and Downtown Skyport. Abbott was born in Springfield, Ohio, in 1898; in Paris she became an assistant to Man Ray, who introduced her to Eugène Atget's photographs in 1925. In 1935 she was hired by the Federal Art Project as a project supervisor and used a large format camera to photograph the city. Commons treats the picture as the work of a WPA employee, in the public domain.
feed.lookAt: Abbott stands at the end of a pier, and its edge leads the eye straight into a canyon of towers. Tall buildings pointing up, a sliver of sky and cloud between them, and a low level camera keep the verticals straight. Find a long foreground line that points into your subject.

caption.title: Manhattan Skyline, South Street and Jones Lane
caption.line2: Berenice Abbott · New York Public Library

feed.title: Mount Batok from Bromo

image.credit: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: From Brahma, Hindu god of creation

feed.story: Mount Batok is the neighbouring cone that is often mistaken for Mount Bromo because of its prominence in the Tengger caldera. Bromo itself stands at 2,329 metres in the middle of a plain called the Sea of Sand, in a nature reserve protected since 1919. It is not the highest peak of the massif but is the most active and famous. The name Bromo comes from the Javanese pronunciation of Brahma, the Hindu god of creation. Bromo erupted in 2004, and two people were killed by rocks thrown out in that episode, and it began to erupt violently again on 26 November 2010. This photograph shows Batok in early-morning light, taken from the peak of Bromo's cone at 05:39 on 20 August 2022.
feed.lookAt: Low sun lights only Batok's slopes, so its fluted gullies glow orange against a deep blue sky and run like lines down the cone. The dark crater rim in the foreground gives the glowing cone depth, and a pale plume and low mist soften the background. Be on the rim before sunrise.

feed.title: Tara Cathedrals

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Tara salt flat lies in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. The Salar de Tara reserve is in the commune of San Pedro de Atacama, Antofagasta Region, and covers 740 square kilometres in seven separate sections. In the Tara and Aguas Calientes area the terrain reaches up to 4,860 metres above sea level. The reserve was designated a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention in 1996. Its wildlife includes several flamingo species, which are classed as vulnerable, along with endangered species such as the vicuña and Darwin's rhea, and it is managed by the Corporación Nacional Forestal. This panorama, taken at 12:01 on 7 February 2016, shows the Tara Cathedrals on the left and the salt flat.
feed.lookAt: Midday sun is usually a problem, but here the cumulus clouds do the work: they build a high, textured sky over the green wetland and the pale lake. The red rock spires sit small on the left, balanced by the clouds on the right. At f/11 on a 24 mm lens, everything from bushes to far mountains stays sharp.

feed.title: Johnstown Housing, Pennsylvania

image.credit: Walker Evans, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Walker Evans made this photograph of housing in Johnstown, Pennsylvania, in December 1935, as part of his work for the Resettlement and Farm Security Administration. The Library of Congress holds it under digital IDs fsa.8c52080 and cph.3c03098. Evans was born in St. Louis, Missouri, and quickly turned a temporary job into a full-time position as an information specialist. The majority of his New Deal photography used a large format 8 × 10 inch view camera. He said his goal was to make pictures that are "literate, authoritative, transcendent", and in a 1964 Yale lecture he described his own style as "Lyric Documentary".
feed.lookAt: From a vantage above the town, a view camera records every roof, porch and fence rail with equal sharpness. A dusting of snow outlines the roofs and the slope, so the rooftops repeat in a pattern from the bottom edge to the top. Find a high viewpoint and let one repeating shape fill the frame.

feed.title: Eilean Donan at Sunrise

image.credit: Diliff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Meeting of Lochs Duich, Long and Alsh

feed.story: Eilean Donan is a small tidal island at the confluence of three sea lochs: Loch Duich, Loch Long and Loch Alsh. The original castle was built in the thirteenth century and became a stronghold of the Clan Mackenzie and their allies, the Clan MacRae. Royal Naval ships destroyed it in 1719, and the castle was demolished by the gunpowder exploding. By 1912 very little of it was still standing. Between 1919 and 1932 it was rebuilt by Lt. Col. John MacRae-Gilstrap, and the present buildings are entirely the result of that 20th-century reconstruction, which included an arched bridge for easier access. This view from the south-east at sunrise was taken on 6 January 2011 as a 2×6 segment panorama.
feed.lookAt: Low winter sun strikes the castle's stone and turns it gold while the cloud behind stays dark, so the building glows against its backdrop. The calm tidal water repeats that glow below. The bridge arches lead in from the right. Shoot when the water is still and the sun is low enough to light only the walls.

feed.title: Giant Wild Goose Pagoda

image.credit: Alexey Komarov, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda is a seven-storey Buddhist pagoda in the Daci'en Temple complex in southern Xi'an, Shaanxi, China. In 652, during the Tang dynasty, the monk Xuanzang oversaw its construction to preserve the hundreds of Sanskrit scriptures he had brought back from India. The original tower had five storeys; under Wu Zetian it was rebuilt as a seven-storey square pavilion-style tower. It is built of brick, and its present exterior mainly reflects major Ming-dynasty work. Its total height, including the base, is 64.1 metres. By 1996 it leaned about one metre, and groundwater control later helped it recover. This photograph was taken at 18:02 on 22 May 2018.
feed.lookAt: Shooting straight up the façade from its base makes the vertical lines converge, and each projecting eave becomes a heavy horizontal band that repeats up the tower. Cropping out the surroundings leaves only brick, shadow and blue sky. Warm late sun deepens the brick. Get close, point up, and let the repetition be the picture.

feed.title: Old Cable Ferry, Alabama

image.credit: Marion Post Wolcott, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Marion Post Wolcott photographed this old cable ferry between Camden and Gees Bend, Alabama, for the Farm Security Administration. The Library of Congress dates it "May 1939?", with a question mark, and holds it as fsa.8a40088. Wolcott was born in Montclair, New Jersey, on 7 June 1910; Stryker was impressed by her work and hired her immediately. Her FSA photographs often explore the political aspects of poverty and deprivation. She resigned in February 1942 after marrying Leon Oliver Wolcott and died in Santa Barbara, California, in 1990. The version on Wikimedia Commons was restored by Adam Cuerden.
feed.lookAt: The camera faces the low light across the river, so the water becomes a pale sheet and the far trees a dark band. The ferry sits as a silhouette, with a man holding a pole at its edge, and the cable slants across the sky to tie the frame together. Shoot toward the light and expose for the sky.

caption.title: Old Cable Ferry, Alabama
caption.line2: Marion Post Wolcott · Library of Congress

feed.title: Hassan Tower

image.credit: Petar Milošević, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Hassan Tower is the minaret of an incomplete mosque in Rabat, Morocco. It was commissioned by Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur, the third caliph of the Almohad Caliphate, and construction began in 1191. When al-Mansur died in 1199, work on the mosque stopped. The tower is 44 metres tall, though its intended height was at least 64 metres. It is made of sandstone and has a square plan measuring 16 metres per side, while the mosque's walls were lime concrete on a rubble stone base. The mosque also sustained some damage in the 1755 Lisbon earthquake. The site was granted World Heritage status in 2012 as part of historic Rabat. This photograph was taken on 27 March 2024.
feed.lookAt: A palm trunk climbs the left of the frame while the tower fills the right: two vertical shapes, one soft and curved, one hard and square. The saturated blue sky and the sandstone's warm tone are near-complementary. The red wall along the bottom anchors the picture. Look for a foreground object whose shape answers your main subject.

feed.title: Himeji Castle

image.credit: Martin Falbisoner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: 46.4 m high, six floors and a basement

feed.story: Himeji Castle is a hilltop Japanese castle complex in Himeji, a city in Hyōgo Prefecture, often known as White Egret Castle or White Heron Castle. Himeyama hill was first fortified in 1333 by Akamatsu Norimura. Tokugawa Ieyasu granted the castle to his son-in-law Ikeda Terumasa, who completely rebuilt and expanded it from 1601 to 1609. The main keep is 46.4 metres high, standing 92 metres above sea level, and has six floors and a basement. In World War II, although most of the surrounding area was burned to the ground, the castle survived intact, and it again survived the 1995 earthquake virtually undamaged. It was registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 11 December 1993. This photograph was taken on 17 November 2016.
feed.lookAt: The stone wall and the white plaster wall in the lower half form a long horizontal that crosses the frame and holds the keep high in the upper right. Red autumn leaves frame it on the left. Using wall and moat as foreground gives the castle a sense of height, defence and distance.

feed.title: The Himalaya from the Space Station

image.credit: Jeff Williams, NASA, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: NASA astronaut Jeff Williams took this view of the Himalaya from the International Space Station on 30 April 2016, and posted about "the amazing array of white peaks on the Himalaya Mountains". NASA's Johnson Space Center catalogues it as ISS047-E-087333. The camera was a Nikon D4 at a 1,150 mm focal length, 1/2,000 second, f/11 and ISO 250, and the Commons file was re-rendered from NASA's raw image data. Williams, born on 18 January 1958, is a retired United States Army officer and former NASA astronaut. He was selected in 1996, became commander of Expedition 48, and his cumulative 534 days in space beat Scott Kelly's total.
feed.lookAt: At 1,150 mm the station window becomes a telescope, flattening hundreds of kilometres of ridges into stacked bands. Haze near the horizon turns blue, then black space sits above it, so distance reads as colour. Side light picks out snow and shade. With a long lens, aim along a range and let haze separate the layers.

caption.title: The Himalaya from the Space Station

feed.title: Hanging Temple, Hunyuan

image.credit: Zhangzhugang, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Hanging Temple, also called the Hanging Monastery or Xuankong Temple, is built into a cliff 75 metres above the ground near Mount Heng, in Hunyuan County, Datong City, Shanxi Province, China. Wikipedia says its construction was started at the end of the Northern Wei dynasty by one man, a monk named Liaoran. It integrates Confucianism, Buddhism and Taoism. The temple relies on 27 wooden beams to support all the main buildings, and oak crossbeams are fitted into holes chiselled into the cliff. It has 40 halls and pavilions in all. The closest city is Datong, 64 kilometres to the northwest. This photograph was taken at 09:02 on 30 August 2013.
feed.lookAt: The cliff overhang dominates the frame, which is the point: the temple looks small and fragile beneath all that rock. The pale, flat rock face gives the red and gold roofs strong contrast. Include plenty of cliff and the thin red supports, and let the proportions explain why the building is remarkable.

feed.title: Longsheng Rice Terraces

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Longji Rice Terraces are in the town of Longji in Longsheng Various Nationalities Autonomous County, about 100 kilometres from Guilin. They lie between 600 and 800 metres above sea level, and the terraced fields were mostly built about 650 years ago. Longji is given in English as "Dragon's Spine", while Longsheng means "Dragon's Victory". Each season changes them, with layers of water in spring, layers of green rice shoots in summer, layers of rice in fall and layers of frost in winter. In early June, water is pumped over the rice paddies and young plants are moved to the main terraces. This photograph was taken on 22 November 2017, in Longsheng County, Guangxi.
feed.lookAt: The curving terrace edges are the subject: each one is a contour line, and from above they repeat in arcs that sweep the eye through the frame. Late-autumn stubble gives a muted gold-and-olive palette, and the grasses in front add depth. Look for a viewpoint high enough that the contour lines stack.

feed.title: Northern India at Night

image.credit: NASA, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Astronauts on the International Space Station made this long exposure of Northern India on 18 January 2016, while the Earth was shrouded in darkness. North is on the upper right, where the snowcapped Himalaya and the Tibetan plateau may be seen. Major cities in view include New Delhi, on the right side of the image, and Lahore on the left. NASA's Johnson Space Center catalogues it as ISS046-E-012758. It was shot on a Nikon D4 with a 28 mm lens at f/1.4, 1/3 second and ISO 10,000, and is a Featured Picture on Commons. An annotated version marks about 40 features, including Jaipur, Srinagar, Kabul and Tashkent, and an airglow layer.
feed.lookAt: At ISO 10,000, f/1.4 and a third of a second, city lights become glowing clusters joined by thin lines of roads. A pale cloud layer catches the glow, a green airglow band curves along the horizon, and stars sit above it. Use a steady support, open the lens wide and expose only long enough to record the lights.

feed.title: Sun and Moon Pagodas

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Sun and Moon Pagodas stand in Guilin, Guangxi, China. They were originally built in the city moat of Guilin during the Tang dynasty and were reconstructed in 2001. The Sun Pagoda is faced with bronze, has nine stories and is 41 metres tall, and is described as the tallest bronze pagoda in the world. The Moon Pagoda is faced with glazed tile, has seven stories and is 35 metres tall, and stands on an island in Shan Lake. The two are linked by an underwater glass tunnel. This photograph, taken on 21 November 2017, is an HDR composed of three exposures of 1/2, 2 and 8 seconds at f/11.
feed.lookAt: The lit towers are far brighter than the dark water and sky, so one exposure cannot hold both; here three exposures, from half a second to 8 seconds, were blended. The still lake then repeats every colour as a long reflection. Use a tripod, bracket your exposures and wait for calm water.

feed.title: The Monastery, Petra

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ad Deir, whose Arabic name ed-Deir means "The Monastery", is a rock-cut monument high in the hills northwest of the Petra city centre, in Jordan. The Deir was probably carved in the mid-first century AD, and its dedication is listed as Obodas I, with a question mark marking it as uncertain. The rock-cut façade is 47 metres high and 48 metres wide, and the door to the main chamber is 8 metres high. The monastery can be reached by ascending a path of nearly 800 steps, a 40-minute walk from the Basin. This photograph, taken on 30 September 2011, shows the façade carved into the sandstone hill.
feed.lookAt: Hard sun from the front-left models every column and carved shadow, while the cloudless sky is a clean blue backdrop. The sandstone's warm tones and the blue are near-complementary, so the monument separates cleanly. Bright, direct light suits carved surfaces; shoot when it skims across them.

feed.title: Interior of Grand Central

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith photographed this interior of Grand Central Station in 2007; the Library of Congress title is Interior, Grand Central Station, New York, New York (highsm.04087). It was a gift and purchase from Highsmith in 2009, part of her America project, and she has donated her photographs to the Library since 1992 to create a copyright-free and royalty-free archive. Grand Central Terminal is a commuter rail terminal at 42nd Street and Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan. It opened on 2 February 1913 and has 44 platforms, more than any other railroad station in the world. Its concourse is 35,000 square feet, and Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis helped ward off its demolition.
feed.lookAt: A slow shutter turns commuters into soft ghosts on the polished floor, so the building stays calm while the crowd moves. Centring the camera on the three arched windows keeps the hall symmetrical, and the green ceiling fills the top. In a busy interior, use a tripod and a long exposure.

caption.title: Interior of Grand Central
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Tunnel View, Yosemite Valley

image.credit: Diliff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Yosemite Valley, in Yosemite National Park, California, is about 12 kilometres long and 910 to 1,070 metres deep. For the last 30 million years glaciers have periodically filled much of the valley, and the youngest of its plutons is the 87-million-year-old Half Dome granodiorite. Bridalveil Fall drops 190 metres. Wikipedia notes that the first view of Yosemite Valley many visitors see is Tunnel View, which is where this photograph was taken on 16 May 2013. El Capitan stands on the left, a dome rises in the distance, and Bridalveil Fall drops down the cliffs on the right.
feed.lookAt: Tunnel View works because the valley is framed on both sides: El Capitan's grey wall on the left, the cliffs beside Bridalveil Fall on the right, and dark forest filling the bottom. That V-shape points the eye to the distant dome. Look for a viewpoint where the near walls act as a frame.

feed.title: Uçhisar Castle

image.credit: Wolfgang Moroder, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Uçhisar is a town in Nevşehir Province in Cappadocia, Turkey, 7 kilometres east of Nevşehir. Its name means "outer citadel" in Turkish and refers to the huge rock cone that is its central feature. The town is dominated by a 60-metre-high "castle" that is actually a rock formation visible over a wide distance. It was cut out of tuff in earlier times and is crisscrossed by numerous underground passageways and rooms. The town stands at 1,270 metres above sea level. Like most of Cappadocia, Uçhisar once made a living from agriculture but now depends almost entirely on tourism. This photograph of the castle was taken on 21 April 2014.
feed.lookAt: Warm side light picks out hundreds of windows and doorways in the rock, so the cone reads as inhabited rather than merely rocky. The pinnacle at left leans toward the castle and makes a second shape that leads the eye up to the flag. Move until two rock forms overlap, then wait for sun on both.
